hints: Look closely at the connectivity first, then focus on the spatial arrangement around the double bonds.
Check the C=C bearing the $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ group, notice the $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and H swap sides between geraniol and nerol.
Recall which type of stereoisomerism arises from restricted rotation about a C=C with two different groups on each carbon.
walkthrough:
**Check if the skeleton is the same**

Both molecules have the same carbon chain, the same two C=C positions and the same $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$ group on the same carbon. So this is not a structural difference in skeleton or position.

Connectivity: same $\text{C}_{10}$ chain with $\text{-OH}$ in same place

**Zoom in on the key double bond**

Look at the upper C=C in each structure. Each C has two different groups. On the left C: $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2-$. On the right C: $\text{H}$ and $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$.

$$ \text{C}(\text{CH}_3)(\text{R}) = \text{C}(\text{H})(\text{CH}_2\text{OH}) $$

**Compare the spatial arrangement**

In geraniol the two larger groups ($\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2-$ and $\text{-CH}_2\text{OH}$) are on opposite sides of the double bond, the trans arrangement. In nerol they are on the same side, the cis arrangement. Restricted rotation about C=C locks this in.

Conclusion: same structural formula, different geometry in space, so geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism.

options.A: Chain isomerism needs a different arrangement of the carbon skeleton, such as straight vs branched. Here both have the identical branched 10-carbon skeleton, so this is not chain isomerism.
options.B: Correct. Both have the same connectivity but differ in the 3D arrangement around the C=C with $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. Geraniol is the trans (E) form and nerol is the cis (Z) form. This is classic geometrical isomerism due to restricted rotation.
options.C: Optical isomerism needs a chiral centre (a carbon with four different groups) and non-superimposable mirror images. Neither molecule has a chiral centre, and the difference is across a planar double bond, not a mirror image pair.
options.D: Positional isomerism needs the functional group or double bond in a different position along the chain. Here the $\text{-OH}$ group and both C=C bonds are in exactly the same positions, only their spatial orientation differs.
